rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Test a large temperature change at the same gradient to probe selectivity in the central cluster and late doublet. All peaks currently elute well before 10 minutes, leaving room for a shallower gradient afterward.

Halve the gradient slope at the more promising temperature to expand the crowded regions and test slope-dependent selectivity. The current elution window leaves substantial room before the 10-minute time penalty.

Further flatten the gradient to improve the sole remaining critical pair while preserving the resolved central cluster. The last peak at 8.12 minutes leaves room for this modest increase without an expected time penalty.

The shallower gradient drove the remaining critical pair toward co-elution, so return to the best slope and test temperature selectivity. A 5 °C decrease may separate that pair while retaining adequate resolution in the central cluster.

At 60 °C, slightly steepening the best gradient should move the late critical pair away from its co-elution point. The central pairs have modest resolution margins that may accommodate this change, potentially resolving all peaks in under 8 minutes.

This increases the gradient slope only slightly, from 0.04444 to 0.045 organic fraction per minute, targeting the remaining R = 1.49 pair while preserving the central pairs. All peaks should elute before the lower endpoint is reached, making this a fine slope adjustment on the allowed grid.

Injection 7 reached the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark and test a shorter elution window. Raising both endpoints by 0.05 preserves the gradient slope while probing whether all peaks can remain resolved at earlier retention times.

Keep the earlier elution window but flatten the gradient to recover resolution in the central cluster. This tests whether the higher starting organic fraction can yield a fully resolved method faster than injection 7.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction improves central-cluster selectivity enough to tolerate a steeper gradient and shorten the fully resolved separation. Injection 7 remains the maximum-score benchmark.

The high-temperature region has narrow resolution margins, so probe the opposite temperature limit for a different selectivity pattern. This broad, fast gradient will show whether a shorter fully resolved separation is possible at lower temperature.

Modestly flatten the low-temperature gradient to test whether both unresolved pairs improve. The 6.34-minute last peak leaves room to gain resolution while potentially remaining faster than the fully resolved benchmark.

The low-temperature central pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a steeper gradient for a faster separation. Raising temperature slightly also probes whether the late critical pair can separate through a selectivity change.
Lower temperature at the fast gradient to test whether the central cluster opens sufficiently. Comparing directly with injection 13 will also quantify the trade-off in the late pair’s resolution.

Test a shallower gradient beyond the central pair’s apparent crossing region, using a higher starting organic fraction to limit retention time. At 30 °C the late pair showed useful selectivity, making this a candidate for an alternative fully resolved method.
Flatten the gradient further to move the near-coeluting central pair beyond its crossing point. The other pairs have substantial resolution margins, and the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Test whether lowering temperature separates the remaining early critical pair at this slope. This isolates temperature selectivity while retaining the maximum-score method from injection 7 as the benchmark.

Raise both endpoints by 0.05 while preserving the slope of the newly resolved low-temperature method. This tests whether its separation can be shifted earlier without losing the critical pair’s resolution.

The central pair moved toward a crossing when the starting organic fraction increased. Test beyond that crossing at the same slope to seek a faster resolved separation, while retaining injection 7 as the maximum-score benchmark.
Injection 19 achieves maximum CRF with useful resolution margins. Shorten its gradient to reduce the elution time, checking whether the central and late critical pairs remain above R = 1.5.
Shorten the gradient by one grid step from the fastest fully resolved method. The remaining resolution margins suggest this may preserve CRF 1.000 while reducing the last-peak time further.

Test one further shortening step to locate the resolution limit. Injection 21 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark; if either critical pair falls below R = 1.5, retain its gentler slope for refinement.

Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature by one step to test a further reduction in retention time. This probes temperature selectivity without the steeper slope that caused resolution loss in injection 22.

Return to 25 °C and test a higher starting organic fraction with a gentler slope to counter compression of the central cluster. This may shift the separation earlier while preserving full resolution; injection 21 remains the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Use the final injection to test an intermediate slope between the fully resolved 12-minute gradient and the under-resolved 10-minute gradient. This refines the speed–resolution boundary; injection 21 remains the fastest proven method with CRF 1.000.
